overview: This event is about understanding what the airplane can structurally tolerate before you ask it to recover. Be ready to explain how the Vn diagram drives maneuvering-speed decisions, why abrupt or multi-axis inputs can still overstress the aircraft, and how to brief an emergency procedure all the way from recognition to landing or ejection logic.

studyNotes.headline: Discussion items

items.text: The T-6B Vn diagram is the picture that ties airspeed, load factor, stall margin, and structural limits together. If you understand this diagram, accelerated stalls and overstress are no longer separate topics; they are just different ways to leave the safe part of the envelope.

children.text: The left side of the diagram is the stall boundary, where the wing simply cannot produce the lift you are demanding.
The upper and lower boundaries are structural load limits, where the airplane may still be flying but the airframe is no longer being treated kindly.
Flap configuration changes the available lift and stall speed, but it does not make the airplane structurally invincible.

items.text: What the diagram is showing you:

children.text: Low airspeed is not required for a stall. A hard pull at high airspeed can still drive the wing past critical AOA.
The FTI example is worth remembering: a sharp pull at about 200 KIAS can produce an accelerated stall around the 5 G region even though the 1 G stall speed is much lower.
That is why steep turns, downhill recoveries, and panicked pullouts deserve the same respect as obvious slow-flight stall setups.
Know where stall, overstress, and maneuvering-speed logic meet on the same graph.
Be able to explain why load factor increases stall speed and why the answer to an accelerated stall is unloading the wing, not pulling harder.

items.text: Maneuvering speed is the highest airspeed at which a full control deflection in one axis should stall the airplane before it structurally overstresses it. It is not permission to make violent multi-axis inputs and assume the airplane will sort itself out.

children.text: VO is 227 KIAS.
Above VO, a full or abrupt control input in one axis can cause structural damage before the aircraft stalls.
Full rudder above 150 KIAS exceeds rudder system limits even if you are still below VO.
Below VO, the protection only applies to one-axis full deflection. It is not a blanket shield against every abrupt control combination.

Use maneuvering speed as a control-discipline reminder during aerobatics, unusual-attitude recoveries, and any downhill acceleration where you may be tempted to snatch the airplane back to the horizon.
The rudder limit matters because startled feet at higher airspeeds can damage the aircraft long before the rest of the recovery looks obviously bad.
Students often memorize 227 KIAS but forget the one-axis condition that makes the rule true.
The other common miss is treating rudder like a free control at any airspeed. It is not.

items.text: Acceleration limitations are the practical extension of the Vn diagram. They answer the question: what actually bends the airplane when the workload spikes?

children.text: Abrupt full control movement in more than one axis can overstress the aircraft even below VO.
Heavy buffet and rapidly building G are warnings to unload and re-sort, not signs that you should keep pulling until the airplane obeys.
Any high-speed recovery should be flown smoothly enough that you stay ahead of airspeed, G, and rudder limitations together.
Accelerated stalls often begin when a pilot tries to save altitude with a hard pull instead of reducing AOA.
A nose-low recovery, spin recovery pullout, or aerobatic downhill segment can all become acceleration-limit problems if the control inputs are abrupt.
The correct mindset is smooth unload, controlled re-entry into the safe envelope, then rebuild the picture instead of forcing it all at once.
Be able to connect acceleration limits back to maneuvering speed and the Vn diagram rather than briefing them as isolated trivia.
If the explanation never mentions load factor, AOA, and control-input smoothness, it is too shallow.

items.text: Treat this as a cumulative oral spot check. The instructor may choose any emergency procedure and expect you to brief it from recognition through the decision branch that ends in continuation, landing, forced landing, or ejection.

children.text: Start with the recognition cue, then the memory items, then the associated N/W/Cs. Do not jump straight to rote steps.

After the immediate action, be ready to explain what changes the plan: altitude, controllability, engine response, field options, and whether the problem is becoming a PEL, forced-landing, or ejection scenario.
If the EP is critical-action, know the first actions cold enough that you are not using the checklist as a first-look crutch.

Representative study set: Fire on Ground, Emergency Engine Shutdown on the Ground, Emergency Ground Egress, CFS and Ejection CRM, Abort Takeoff, Aircraft Departs Prepared Surface, Engine Failure Immediately After Takeoff, Engine Failure During Flight, Immediate Air-Start, PMU NORM Air-Start, PMU OFF Air-Start, and Uncommanded Power Changes/LOP.
Your goal is not to memorize one instructor's favorite EP list. It is to show that any previously taught FAM emergency can be briefed cleanly and accurately.
If you can only recite steps but cannot explain when to land immediately, continue to a field, or eject, you are not actually ready for this question.
Keep the EP language readable and exact. This event should feel like a clean oral-review standard, not like a pile of disconnected memory items.

studyNotes.summary: Understand how flight loads, maneuvering speed, and control inputs interact, then be able to brief any previously taught FAM emergency procedure with real branch logic.

summary: Vn diagram, maneuvering-speed logic, acceleration limits, and cumulative EP review.
title: Flight Loads and Emergency Review
